questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: ListAgents

Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

397	## 10. Delivery plan and acceptance criteria
398	
399	### Spike 22 — `spikes/22-remote-port`
400	
401	Before any host code, with measured results in its README:
402	
403	- A blocking HTTPS server over `std::net::TcpListener` with `rustls` and an `rcgen` certificate, a WebSocket upgrade with `tungstenite`, and requests handed to a stand-in "frame" thread over a bounded `mpsc`, as the control socket does. Measure request latency through the handoff at the app's frame rate while hidden.
404	- **Frame cost, measured, with targets.** The frame's share of a metadata request, a content handle lookup, a worker's version action and the read-model diff over a few hundred records, each timed per pass; the target is under 1 ms per pass for the port's whole share, and under 4 ms at the 99th percentile with 8 requests in a pass. The content work on the connection thread timed separately: the largest transcript in the user's data directory parsed and masked (its time and peak memory are the supported size for §4.3), a 768 KiB file read and masked, a Keychain read made slow (a locked keychain) and shown to stall only its connection. A stalled subscriber and 20 connections that stall after the TLS handshake, with a healthy paired client and the frame loop measured through both. The README records the numbers and the thresholds, and a pass that misses the target is a design finding, not a tuning note.
405	- **Content versions.** The signals of §4.4 against the cases that defeat weaker ones: a same-size in-place rewrite of a pinned file with mtime restored by `touch -r`, a replace-by-rename, a run log truncated and regrown to the same length, a transcript appended within one poll interval; each must move the version. The two-second `stat` poll over 128 keys timed.
406	- Bonjour advertisement from the Rust process on macOS, visible to a visionOS simulator; the crate or system path that works.
407	- `URLSession` and `URLSessionWebSocketTask` on visionOS accepting the self-signed certificate through a pinning delegate that checks the SPKI hash and nothing weaker; the same delegate refusing a substituted certificate.
408	- The `openat` walk of §4.3 through `rustix` or `cap-std`: a pinned FIFO with no writer refused at once on its connection thread while the frame loop and a second connection keep going; a parent directory swapped for a symlink mid-walk refused.
409	- Two instances on one machine (`SWITCHBOARD_DATA_DIR`, `SWITCHBOARD_TMUX_SOCKET=switchboard-test-*`, different ports) each advertising with its own key.
410	
411	Loopback-only and no auth are fine here and nowhere else.
412	
413	**Results (2026-10-12, `spikes/22-remote-port/README.md`).** The host
414	half ran: the frame's share is under 0.25 ms per pass against the 1 ms
415	target; a request's latency is one frame interval, since a client that
416	sends on the reply synchronizes with the frame; the pools, the 5 s
417	handshake timeout and the subscriber overflow behave as §4.1 says under
418	20 stalled connections and an unread socket, with a paired client
419	unaffected; a wrong pin fails at the handshake; `mdns-sd` advertises

Endpoints: `/info`, `/pair`, projects, spaces, sets, one set, sessions, session, waiting, screen. No events yet; a reply carries `epoch` and `revision` from the counter, which only the diff of A3 will move. 466

471	## 11. Tests and failure cases
472	
473	Host, in `tests/remote.rs` and the adapter's own tests unless said otherwise:
474	
475	- Two hosts produce the same `RecordId` (seeded in fakes): no collision in UI or routing (client).
476	- A host's IP changes; Bonjour rediscovers it under the same pinned key (client, spike).
477	- Two advertisements claim one `server_id` with different keys: no automatic trust or merge (client).
478	- A substituted certificate during first pairing: the client refuses to send the code; and a `/pair` carrying another host's `spki_sha256` is refused by the host.
479	- Three wrong codes from three concurrent connections close the one pairing window; a fourth, correct, is refused. A consumed code is refused on the next `/pair`. Twenty unauthenticated connections and a `/pair` flood past the per-minute cap: a paired client's requests are answered throughout, the flood gets 429 and closed sockets.
480	- After Revoke, the device's next request fails and its WebSocket is closed. After a key rotation, `devices.json` is empty, every old token fails, and the dialog says the pairings are gone; the client, seeing the new key under a known `server_id`, sends nothing and asks to pair again.
481	- A scope lowered in the dialog refuses the device's next `send`; raised, allows it; no request over the port changes a scope.
482	- A mutation dispatched between a subscriber's `hello` and its first snapshot, and another during a multi-resource sync: the client ends with the host's state (host test on the ordering, client test on the reconciliation).
483	- An older snapshot reply arriving after a newer one is dropped by revision (client).
484	- The host restarts: the new `epoch` makes the client refetch everything.
485	- A `send` whose process is killed after the keys went into the pane and before the reply line (the fake host records the write, the fake log fails the reply append): the retry with the same op is answered `interrupted` and nothing is sent twice. A failed request-line append refuses the send and sends nothing. A dropped HTTP response after a logged reply is answered from the log.
486	- `unknown` for an op that never reached the frame; a resubmit runs once.
487	- The configured secret appears in a prompt, a tool result, a final response, a run's output, and a pinned non-dotenv text file: every content endpoint returns it masked. A secret store that fails makes every content endpoint refuse rather than answer.
488	- The configured secret straddles each cut: the parser's `DETAIL_CAP` inside a tool result, the 256 KiB turn cut, the first byte of a run-output tail window, and the front cut of a last response: each reply masks it whole or drops it whole, never a fragment.

492	- Frame cost (F4): a 20 MiB transcript, a 768 KiB file and a Keychain read made to block for two seconds, each requested while a second connection reads session metadata: the metadata reply arrives within a pass and the frame's time per pass stays under its budget; only the requesting connection waits. 493	- A window on the last response alone, and one on the conversation, each refresh when the transcript grows with no session metadata change; a handle rebind refreshes both.

495	- A watched session's transcript grows and a watched pinned file is edited while the host shows an unrelated project, a document, the Dispatch page, and while the window is hidden: `changed` arrives within the poll interval.
496	- A space rename, a session moved between projects, a project and a session removed, a time-based rule set losing a member: the right `changed` and `removed` events, no reconnect.

512	## 12. Answers to the first draft's questions
513	
514	1. **Models and ids.** `src/core/model.rs`: `SessionRecord` (`RecordId`), `Project` (`ProjectId`), `WorkingSet` (`SetId`) with `PinnedItem { target: PinTarget, rect: GridRect }`, `CardState`, `Run` (a command's or service's run with its scrollback log name). Conversations are `ports::transcript::Conversation` with `Turn { n, user, activity, final_text, .. }`, read by `adapters/transcript.rs` from Claude Code's JSONL.
515	2. **Control port reuse.** Yes, directly: `app.rs::serve` takes a `wire::Request` and returns a `wire::Reply`; `core/control.rs` maps bodies to `ControlAction`. The remote adapter is another producer of requests for the same path, with auth, the allowlist and redaction in front, and the log-before-run step added to `serve` for non-replayable commands.
516	3. **Runtime.** None to own; the frame thread is the executor and `listen`/`serve_pending` are the startup and polling hooks. Shutdown drops the listener as the control socket does.
517	4. **Events.** No bus, and no effect that reliably marks a visible change: `Save`, `SaveViews` and `SaveSettings` are three effects, and `PromptSeen` and the quiet interval in `reconcile.rs` change a card with none of them. So the port diffs the exported read models after every pass, with the clock-derived `quiet_secs` held out of the hash, and versions content where it is read (§4.4). Retained replay is not needed: a subscriber is registered on the frame thread, so subscribe-then-snapshot has no gap.
518	5. **Pinned file access.** The document preview (`ui::document::Preview::load`) is a UI loader: a metadata check and then an unbounded read, which is fine for the user's own click and not for a remote reader. The port gets `read_pinned` in the files adapter: a descriptor-anchored `openat` walk with no symlink followed and a nonblocking open, as §4.3 says, run on the connection thread.
519	6. **Per-session UI state and polling.** `UiState` (drafts, scroll, folds) is transient and never read by the core; none of it crosses to the client. The app also parses a transcript synchronously on the frame (`refresh_conversation`), which one frame absorbs for one session on screen and would not for every watched session. The port therefore needs its own watch set, the cache lifted to the app, and content work on the connection and worker threads, which are the app-level changes the implementation constraint allows.
520	7. **Two installations.** `SWITCHBOARD_DATA_DIR` and `SWITCHBOARD_TMUX_SOCKET` on a `switchboard-test-*` socket; only the lock holder listens; `tests/control.rs` and `tests/gate.rs` show the pattern.
521	
522	**Implementation constraint:** no change to the egui frontend beyond A0's cache move, and no change to how the transcript parser reads or shapes a conversation. The host work is one adapter, additive wire views, a `read_pinned` method on the files port, an additive `read_masked` on the transcript reader (the mask runs inside the existing parse, before its detail cap) and an overlap read in `scrollback`, the content caches, read-model diff, two-step content handoff and watch worker in `app.rs`, the log-before-run step in `serve`, a Settings field or two, and one dialog. Anything larger is proposed separately.

527	|---|---|

529	| Multi-host | Concurrent connections and unified browsing |
530	| Resources | Sessions, projects, working sets with pins, pinned files, runs; no card resource |
531	| Identity | `identity.json` UUID and certificate; key in the Keychain per installation; clients pin the public key |
532	| Discovery | Bonjour and manual endpoints |
533	| Host runtime | Frame-thread dispatch for core state; content work on connection and worker threads; blocking std server with bounded queues; no Tokio |
534	| Contract | The `switchboard-control` wire views, extended additively, behind an allowlist |
535	| Data fetch | HTTPS JSON, every reply stamped with epoch and revision |
536	| Live changes | One WSS per host; read-model diff after every pass, content versions assigned on read, watch worker; `changed`/`removed` events; refetch |

539	| Redaction | One policy over every text leaving the port, run on whole source text before any cut; fail closed |
540	| Caps | Collections answered whole with every string bounded; only the conversation pages; scalar content cut after masking or refused whole; the limit enforced on serialized bytes |

548	| Session execution | Always on the owning host |
549	| Resume | User-initiated only, confirmed on the client |

551	| visionOS layout | Native movable windows |

## 10. Delivery plan and acceptance criteria

### Spike 22 — `spikes/22-remote-port`

Before any host code, with measured results in its README:

- A blocking HTTPS server over `std::net::TcpListener` with `rustls` and an `rcgen` certificate, a WebSocket upgrade with `tungstenite`, and requests handed to a stand-in "frame" thread over a bounded `mpsc`, as the control socket does. Measure request latency through the handoff at the app's frame rate while hidden.
- **Frame cost, measured, with targets.** The frame's share of a metadata request, a content handle lookup, a worker's version action and the read-model diff over a few hundred records, each timed per pass; the target is under 1 ms per pass for the port's whole share, and under 4 ms at the 99th percentile with 8 requests in a pass. The content work on the connection thread timed separately: the largest transcript in the user's data directory parsed and masked (its time and peak memory are the supported size for §4.3), a 768 KiB file read and masked, a Keychain read made slow (a locked keychain) and shown to stall only its connection. A stalled subscriber and 20 connections that stall after the TLS handshake, with a healthy paired client and the frame loop measured through both. The README records the numbers and the thresholds, and a pass that misses the target is a design finding, not a tuning note.
- **Content versions.** The signals of §4.4 against the cases that defeat weaker ones: a same-size in-place rewrite of a pinned file with mtime restored by `touch -r`, a replace-by-rename, a run log truncated and regrown to the same length, a transcript appended within one poll interval; each must move the version. The two-second `stat` poll over 128 keys timed.
- Bonjour advertisement from the Rust process on macOS, visible to a visionOS simulator; the crate or system path that works.
- `URLSession` and `URLSessionWebSocketTask` on visionOS accepting the self-signed certificate through a pinning delegate that checks the SPKI hash and nothing weaker; the same delegate refusing a substituted certificate.
- The `openat` walk of §4.3 through `rustix` or `cap-std`: a pinned FIFO with no writer refused at once on its connection thread while the frame loop and a second connection keep going; a parent directory swapped for a symlink mid-walk refused.
- Two instances on one machine (`SWITCHBOARD_DATA_DIR`, `SWITCHBOARD_TMUX_SOCKET=switchboard-test-*`, different ports) each advertising with its own key.

Loopback-only and no auth are fine here and nowhere else.

**Results (2026-10-12, `spikes/22-remote-port/README.md`).** The host
half ran: the frame's share is under 0.25 ms per pass against the 1 ms
target; a request's latency is one frame interval, since a client that
sends on the reply synchronizes with the frame; the pools, the 5 s
handshake timeout and the subscriber overflow behave as §4.1 says under
20 stalled connections and an unread socket, with a paired client
unaffected; a wrong pin fails at the handshake; `mdns-sd` advertises
and `dns-sd` sees it; the 146 MB largest transcript parses in 290 ms at
575 MB peak, which is why content work is off the frame; ctime and
inode catch the same-size rewrite, the rename and the regrown log. Two
amendments follow: content reads go to **one worker thread** with a
queue rather than each connection thread, so one large parse is in
memory at a time (§4.1 is read with that change), and the Bonjour
instance name carries a short id suffix beside the display name. Not
run: the visionOS pinning delegate and the read-model diff timing.

### Milestone A — Host port and multi-host client foundation

Five commits, each leaving the app running and each with its README and design.md status update. The first user-visible result is a two-host read-only client at A2; nothing waits for the synchronization machinery.

**A0 — The conversation cache in the app.** `UiState.conversations` moves to `SwitchboardApp` as the first content cache, keyed by record id, resume handle and content version; the session, card and workflow views read it through a reference. No port code. Acceptance: the UI tests pass unchanged and the app behaves identically.

**A1 — Identity and an authenticated read-only host.** `identity.json` (id, certificate, `server_name` and the listen preference: off the LAN by default, loopback until enabled), the key in the Keychain under its installation's account, `SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT`. `ports::remote`, `adapters/remote.rs` with the bounds of §4.1 and the two-step content handoff, a fake, the `Effect` and `AppAction` arms, the allowlist, the redaction function. The pairing window and QR code in the settings menu, the paired-devices dialog with scope and Revoke, `devices.json`. Endpoints: `/info`, `/pair`, projects, spaces, sets, one set, sessions, session, waiting, screen. No events yet; a reply carries `epoch` and `revision` from the counter, which only the diff of A3 will move. The screen is answered on the frame as the control port answers it (a pane snapshot, redacted); the worker handoff arrives with the screen cache of A4, since there is nothing to version before it. *Built 2026-10-12; see design.md's remote client status.* Tests: `tests/remote.rs` against a real socket with fakes, modelled on `tests/control.rs`, covering pairing, the pin check, scope, revocation, the allowlist and screen redaction; a UI test for the dialog. Acceptance: a paired `curl` with the pinned certificate reads every view over the LAN; an unpaired one gets `/info` and nothing else.

**A2 — Two hosts and the first client.** Bonjour advertisement and the Linux stub. The Swift protocol, transport with the pinning delegate, `ServerRegistry`, `ConnectionManager`, and a read-only browser of sessions and sets with source labels, refreshing on a timer. *Built 2026-10-12 as the package under `client/` with a command-line browser for the Mac; the app targets come with Milestone B; see design.md's remote client status.* Acceptance: two installations have distinct `server_id`s and keys; Bonjour discovers both; the client pairs with both and connects simultaneously; nothing mixes identifiers; taking one offline leaves the other working and its items visibly stale; a changed IP reconnects under the same pin.

**A3 — Synchronization.** The read-model diff after every pass, the revision counter moving, `changed` and `removed` events for metadata and collections, the WebSocket with `hello`, subscribe-then-snapshot and reconciliation by revision on the client, epoch handling, `resync_required`. `ops` and the log-before-run path in `serve` (no commands yet, but the path is tested here). *Built 2026-10-12; see design.md's remote client status. A global collection's `id` is the empty string; the diff runs only on passes that dispatched something; the `runs` collection waits for its endpoint.* Acceptance: the timer refresh of A2 is gone and every host-side change reaches the client within a pass; the mutation-between-hello-and-snapshot test passes on both sides.

**A4 — Watched content.** The watch set and its worker poll, `watch` and `unwatch` with `watching`, content versions for screen (the other content kinds arrive with Milestone C and use the same cache), eviction, the policy fingerprint in the cache key, the overflow close. *Built 2026-10-12; see design.md's remote client status. The worker reads a pane's whole window so a short read and the poll see one version; the policy is resolved and cached on the frame (cleared by any save or secret change) until Milestone C moves the secret reads off it; a key held only by a subscriber has no read time and goes with its last `unwatch`.* Acceptance: a watched pane's screen updates live while the host shows an unrelated view or is hidden; the abuse tests of §4.1 pass against the real adapter.

Across A1 to A4: README (Layout, dev aids, data directory) and the design.md status section, with the trust boundary's sentence on redacted text added at A1.

### Milestone B — Native visionOS browser

- Grid, list and focus browsing of real sessions and sets from two hosts.
- Two items from different servers open as independent spatial windows.
- Each window offers `compact` and `screen`; the other modes arrive with Milestone C and the window says so until then.
- Closing a window never ends a session.
- Reconnect preserves open windows and refreshes them through subscribe-then-snapshot.

*Built 2026-10-12 on the visionOS simulator, three commits (B1 the app shell on an xcodegen project, B2 card windows, B3 browsing and persistence); see design.md's remote client status. The headset itself waits on the one-time Xcode device setup.*

### Milestone C — Interactive sessions

- `session.conversation`, `session.last_response`, `session.runs`, `session.run_output` and `file.read` on the wire and the port, with `read_pinned` in the files adapter, `read_masked` on the transcript reader and the overlap read in `scrollback`.
- Conversation paging by turn, with the body cap, the oversized turn, the in-progress last turn and the rebind handled.
- `send`, `resume` and `trust` under `control` scope, with the operation id as the idempotency key and `/ops/{op}` on timeout.
- Live updates over the WebSocket through the watch set; scroll and disclosure restoration across incremental refetches and reconnects.
- System dictation into the text field as the initial voice input.

*C1 and C2 built 2026-10-13 (the content endpoints but `file.read`, the conversation paged and merged, the three modes drawn), C3 the same day (`send`, `resume` and `trust` under the control scope through the control socket's `serve` and log, the op the key, `/ops/{op}` on a timeout; a control bar on a Claude session's window with a microphone button that dictates through the Speech framework; the conversation view's place, scroll and folds, kept across merges, reconnects and relaunches); see design.md's remote client status. `file.read` and the policy reads off the frame remain. C4 the same day: `file.read` (`GET projects/{id}/files/{path}`, a file some working set pins, read through the descriptor walk of §4.3 in `adapters::files::open_pinned` on the content worker, versioned by inode, change time and size, masked, refused `not_pinned`, `too_large` with its size, or `failed` for a dotenv file, a symlink or a non-text file) and the policy resolved on the worker: the frame hands the worker what names a policy (`PolicySpec`: the project environment, the sets, an epoch moved by every save and secret change) and the worker reads the dotenv files and the secret store, caching per spec, so a slow Keychain call never costs a frame. Milestone C is complete.*

### Milestone D — Shared iPadOS shell

- The same modules and components on iPad with platform-appropriate navigation and windows.

*Not started; Milestones A to C merged without it (2026-10-14).*

## 11. Tests and failure cases

Host, in `tests/remote.rs` and the adapter's own tests unless said otherwise:

- Two hosts produce the same `RecordId` (seeded in fakes): no collision in UI or routing (client).
- A host's IP changes; Bonjour rediscovers it under the same pinned key (client, spike).
- Two advertisements claim one `server_id` with different keys: no automatic trust or merge (client).
- A substituted certificate during first pairing: the client refuses to send the code; and a `/pair` carrying another host's `spki_sha256` is refused by the host.
- Three wrong codes from three concurrent connections close the one pairing window; a fourth, correct, is refused. A consumed code is refused on the next `/pair`. Twenty unauthenticated connections and a `/pair` flood past the per-minute cap: a paired client's requests are answered throughout, the flood gets 429 and closed sockets.
- After Revoke, the device's next request fails and its WebSocket is closed. After a key rotation, `devices.json` is empty, every old token fails, and the dialog says the pairings are gone; the client, seeing the new key under a known `server_id`, sends nothing and asks to pair again.
- A scope lowered in the dialog refuses the device's next `send`; raised, allows it; no request over the port changes a scope.
- A mutation dispatched between a subscriber's `hello` and its first snapshot, and another during a multi-resource sync: the client ends with the host's state (host test on the ordering, client test on the reconciliation).
- An older snapshot reply arriving after a newer one is dropped by revision (client).
- The host restarts: the new `epoch` makes the client refetch everything.
- A `send` whose process is killed after the keys went into the pane and before the reply line (the fake host records the write, the fake log fails the reply append): the retry with the same op is answered `interrupted` and nothing is sent twice. A failed request-line append refuses the send and sends nothing. A dropped HTTP response after a logged reply is answered from the log.
- `unknown` for an op that never reached the frame; a resubmit runs once.
- The configured secret appears in a prompt, a tool result, a final response, a run's output, and a pinned non-dotenv text file: every content endpoint returns it masked. A secret store that fails makes every content endpoint refuse rather than answer.
- The configured secret straddles each cut: the parser's `DETAIL_CAP` inside a tool result, the 256 KiB turn cut, the first byte of a run-output tail window, and the front cut of a last response: each reply masks it whole or drops it whole, never a fragment.
- A project with three hundred sessions, each with 64 KiB notes and a 100 KiB `name`, listed whole: one reply under the cap, notes cut at 4 KiB and names at 4 KiB with each field in `truncated`, no member lost; the same session read alone carries its notes whole. A session entering and leaving `waiting` emits `changed {waiting}` and the refetched collection lacks or holds it accordingly; a member missing from a whole reply at a later revision is dropped by the client, a member missing from an older reply arriving late is not.
- A 700 KiB file of quotation marks is under the source limit and answers `too_large` from the serialized check; a pane with 200 lines of 4 KiB each is cut by bytes after masking and marked. A pinned file over the source limit answers `too_large`; a last response over the body cap is cut from the front and marked.
- Content versions (F2): a pinned file rewritten in place at the same size with its mtime restored, a file replaced by rename, a run log truncated and regrown to its old length, and a transcript appended twice within one poll interval: each read after the change carries new content and a new revision, and no two different bodies for one key share a revision within an epoch. Two reads of an unchanged file carry the same revision.
- Frame cost (F4): a 20 MiB transcript, a 768 KiB file and a Keychain read made to block for two seconds, each requested while a second connection reads session metadata: the metadata reply arrives within a pass and the frame's time per pass stays under its budget; only the requesting connection waits. A content handle read on the frame for a record removed before the worker finishes: the worker's version action is a no-op and the reply names the handle it read.
- A window on the last response alone, and one on the conversation, each refresh when the transcript grows with no session metadata change; a handle rebind refreshes both.
- With every content cache populated, a new environment-set grant, a changed secret value, and a secret store that starts failing: unchanged screen, file and run-output sources are not served from their old masked bytes; the first two emit `changed` for the watched keys and serve newly masked text, the third refuses.
- A watched session's transcript grows and a watched pinned file is edited while the host shows an unrelated project, a document, the Dispatch page, and while the window is hidden: `changed` arrives within the poll interval.
- A space rename, a session moved between projects, a project and a session removed, a time-based rule set losing a member: the right `changed` and `removed` events, no reconnect.
- A set renamed and a pin moved (saved through `SaveViews`), a Claude Code pane reaching its trust question (`PromptSeen`, no save), and a Codex pane passing its quiet interval (`HostListed`, no save, no screen change): each emits `changed` for the right resource within the pass. Ten passes over a running pane with nothing else moving emit nothing, though `quiet_secs` moved on each.
- Two reads of a watched file, a transcript and a pane separated by an external edit with no poll between them, delivered to the client in reverse order: the client ends on the newer content. A read of a session's metadata between them does not invalidate the conversation page.
- Closing one of two windows on a session sends no `unwatch`; closing the second does. A hundred and twenty-nine watched keys against the cap of 128: the least recently read is evicted, a read of it still answers with the right version and re-enters it, and no watch is refused. Reconnect resends the watches before any snapshot.
- Forget server on the client removes its token, pin, memory and views; a revocation seen on a connection drops the token and memory and keeps the views marked; nothing from a host is found on the client's disk after a relaunch (client).
- The subscriber queue overflows: `resync_required`, the socket closes, the host's frame loop and a second subscriber are unaffected (spike and adapter test).
- 20 stalled unauthenticated connections: the port stays answerable to a paired client (spike).
- `read_pinned`: a pin with `..`, an absolute path, an empty component; a symlink as a parent component (inside or outside the root, both refused) and as the leaf; a parent directory swapped for a symlink between two hops of the walk, driven from a second thread; a file that grows past the limit during the read; a FIFO with no writer, asserting the refusal returns at once and an unrelated request completes meanwhile; a directory and a device as the leaf. Each refused or capped as §4.3 says.
- A long transcript pages by turn; one enormous turn is cut and marked; a conversation whose handle changed answers with the new `resume_id` and the client refetches from 1 (client).
- An exited command whose pane is gone: `screen` refuses, `runs` and `run_output` answer from the log; a pruned log answers with the reason.
- Several windows show one session with independent view state and consistent data (client).
- A request outside the allowlist (`env.resolve`, `project.add`, a path that no set pins, a pinned `.env`) is refused with no side effect, and the refusal is logged by name only.
- Revocation while connected: the WebSocket closes, the next request fails with the reason, cached content stays readable on the client but is marked.
- A restart and a rebuild under the stable signing identity keep the key readable; two data directories under one macOS account keep separate keys; a missing key makes a fresh identity and the dialog says the pairings are gone.
- A `cfg(not(target_os = "macos"))` build compiles with the Bonjour adapter stubbed.

## 12. Answers to the first draft's questions

1. **Models and ids.** `src/core/model.rs`: `SessionRecord` (`RecordId`), `Project` (`ProjectId`), `WorkingSet` (`SetId`) with `PinnedItem { target: PinTarget, rect: GridRect }`, `CardState`, `Run` (a command's or service's run with its scrollback log name). Conversations are `ports::transcript::Conversation` with `Turn { n, user, activity, final_text, .. }`, read by `adapters/transcript.rs` from Claude Code's JSONL.
2. **Control port reuse.** Yes, directly: `app.rs::serve` takes a `wire::Request` and returns a `wire::Reply`; `core/control.rs` maps bodies to `ControlAction`. The remote adapter is another producer of requests for the same path, with auth, the allowlist and redaction in front, and the log-before-run step added to `serve` for non-replayable commands.
3. **Runtime.** None to own; the frame thread is the executor and `listen`/`serve_pending` are the startup and polling hooks. Shutdown drops the listener as the control socket does.
4. **Events.** No bus, and no effect that reliably marks a visible change: `Save`, `SaveViews` and `SaveSettings` are three effects, and `PromptSeen` and the quiet interval in `reconcile.rs` change a card with none of them. So the port diffs the exported read models after every pass, with the clock-derived `quiet_secs` held out of the hash, and versions content where it is read (§4.4). Retained replay is not needed: a subscriber is registered on the frame thread, so subscribe-then-snapshot has no gap.
5. **Pinned file access.** The document preview (`ui::document::Preview::load`) is a UI loader: a metadata check and then an unbounded read, which is fine for the user's own click and not for a remote reader. The port gets `read_pinned` in the files adapter: a descriptor-anchored `openat` walk with no symlink followed and a nonblocking open, as §4.3 says, run on the connection thread.
6. **Per-session UI state and polling.** `UiState` (drafts, scroll, folds) is transient and never read by the core; none of it crosses to the client. The conversation cache in `UiState` and the caption poll in `refresh_captions` both follow the local view: a session not on the Mac's screen is not polled, and a document, workflow, Dispatch or ticket view polls nothing. The app also parses a transcript synchronously on the frame (`refresh_conversation`), which one frame absorbs for one session on screen and would not for every watched session. The port therefore needs its own watch set, the cache lifted to the app, and content work on the connection and worker threads, which are the app-level changes the implementation constraint allows.
7. **Two installations.** `SWITCHBOARD_DATA_DIR` and `SWITCHBOARD_TMUX_SOCKET` on a `switchboard-test-*` socket; only the lock holder listens; `tests/control.rs` and `tests/gate.rs` show the pattern.

**Implementation constraint:** no change to the egui frontend beyond A0's cache move, and no change to how the transcript parser reads or shapes a conversation. The host work is one adapter, additive wire views, a `read_pinned` method on the files port, an additive `read_masked` on the transcript reader (the mask runs inside the existing parse, before its detail cap) and an overlap read in `scrollback`, the content caches, read-model diff, two-step content handoff and watch worker in `app.rs`, the log-before-run step in `serve`, a Settings field or two, and one dialog. Anything larger is proposed separately.

## 13. Explicit design decisions

| Multi-host | Concurrent connections and unified browsing |
| Resources | Sessions, projects, working sets with pins, pinned files, runs; no card resource |
| Identity | `identity.json` UUID and certificate; key in the Keychain per installation; clients pin the public key |
| Discovery | Bonjour and manual endpoints |
| Host runtime | Frame-thread dispatch for core state; content work on connection and worker threads; blocking std server with bounded queues; no Tokio |
| Contract | The `switchboard-control` wire views, extended additively, behind an allowlist |
| Data fetch | HTTPS JSON, every reply stamped with epoch and revision |
| Live changes | One WSS per host; read-model diff after every pass, content versions assigned on read, watch worker; `changed`/`removed` events; refetch |
| Synchronization | Subscribe, then snapshot, then reconcile by revision; full refetch on a new epoch |
| Idempotency | The control port's operation id and `operations.log`, non-replayable commands logged before they run |
| Redaction | One policy over every text leaving the port, run on whole source text before any cut; fail closed |
| Caps | Collections answered whole with every string bounded; only the conversation pages; scalar content cut after masking or refused whole; the limit enforced on serialized bytes |
| Content versions | Transcript: size and mtime (append-only); file and run log: inode, ctime and size; screen: hash; no two bodies share a revision for one key |
| Masked caches | Versioned by source and by the project's redaction policy fingerprint; a resolution failure refuses, never serves a cached success |
| Watch set | Global cap of 128, least recently read evicted, never refused; a read always versions correctly |
| File reads | Descriptor-anchored `openat` walk, no symlink followed, nonblocking open, 768 KiB, on the connection thread |
| Authentication | Pairing window with QR, key verified before the code is sent, 40-bit single-use code with one global attempt counter, 256-bit bearer token without expiry, scope set in the host dialog; Keychain on both ends; key rotation clears every pairing |
| Client storage | Server list and presentation state on disk, token and pin in the Keychain, every host body in memory only |
| Milestone A | Five commits: cache move, authenticated read-only host, two-host client, synchronization, watched content |
| Session execution | Always on the owning host |
| Resume | User-initiated only, confirmed on the client |
| Presentation state | Client-owned |

477	- Two advertisements claim one `server_id` with different keys: no automatic trust or merge (client).
478	- A substituted certificate during first pairing: the client refuses to send the code; and a `/pair` carrying another host's `spki_sha256` is refused by the host.
479	- Three wrong codes from three concurrent connections close the one pairing window; a fourth, correct, is refused. A consumed code is refused on the next `/pair`. 482	- A mutation dispatched between a subscriber's `hello` and its first snapshot, and another during a multi-resource sync: the client ends with the host's state (host test on the ordering, client test on the reconciliation).
483	- An older snapshot reply arriving after a newer one is dropped by revision (client).
484	- The host restarts: the new `epoch` makes the client refetch everything.
485	- A `send` whose process is killed after the keys went into the pane and before the reply line (the fake host records the write, the fake log fails the reply append): the retry with the same op is answered `interrupted` and nothing is sent twice. 512	## 12. Answers to the first draft's questions
513	
514	1. **Models and ids.** `src/core/model.rs`: `SessionRecord` (`RecordId`), `Project` (`ProjectId`), `WorkingSet` (`SetId`) with `PinnedItem { target: PinTarget, rect: GridRect }`, `CardState`, `Run` (a command's or service's run with its scrollback log name). Conversations are `ports::transcript::Conversation` with `Turn { n, user, activity, final_text, .. }`, read by `adapters/transcript.rs` from Claude Code's JSONL.
515	2. **Control port reuse.** Yes, directly: `app.rs::serve` takes a `wire::Request` and returns a `wire::Reply`; `core/control.rs` maps bodies to `ControlAction`. The remote adapter is another producer of requests for the same path, with auth, the allowlist and redaction in front, and the log-before-run step added to `serve` for non-replayable commands.
516	3. **Runtime.** None to own; the frame thread is the executor and `listen`/`serve_pending` are the startup and polling hooks. Shutdown drops the listener as the control socket does.
517	4. **Events.** No bus, and no effect that reliably marks a visible change: `Save`, `SaveViews` and `SaveSettings` are three effects, and `PromptSeen` and the quiet interval in `reconcile.rs` change a card with none of them. So the port diffs the exported read models after every pass, with the clock-derived `quiet_secs` held out of the hash, and versions content where it is read (§4.4). Retained replay is not needed: a subscriber is registered on the frame thread, so subscribe-then-snapshot has no gap.
518	5. **Pinned file access.** The document preview (`ui::document::Preview::load`) is a UI loader: a metadata check and then an unbounded read, which is fine for the user's own click and not for a remote reader. The port gets `read_pinned` in the files adapter: a descriptor-anchored `openat` walk with no symlink followed and a nonblocking open, as §4.3 says, run on the connection thread.
519	6. **Per-session UI state and polling.** `UiState` (drafts, scroll, folds) is transient and never read by the core; none of it crosses to the client. The conversation cache in `UiState` and the caption poll in `refresh_captions` both follow the local view: a session not on the Mac's screen is not polled, and a document, workflow, Dispatch or ticket view polls nothing. The app also parses a transcript synchronously on the frame (`refresh_conversation`), which one frame absorbs for one session on screen and would not for every watched session. The port therefore needs its own watch set, the cache lifted to the app, and content work on the connection and worker threads, which are the app-level changes the implementation constraint allows.
520	7. **Two installations.** `SWITCHBOARD_DATA_DIR` and `SWITCHBOARD_TMUX_SOCKET` on a `switchboard-test-*` socket; only the lock holder listens; `tests/control.rs` and `tests/gate.rs` show the pattern.
521	
522	**Implementation constraint:** no change to the egui frontend beyond A0's cache move, and no change to how the transcript parser reads or shapes a conversation. The host work is one adapter, additive wire views, a `read_pinned` method on the files port, an additive `read_masked` on the transcript reader (the mask runs inside the existing parse, before its detail cap) and an overlap read in `scrollback`, the content caches, read-model diff, two-step content handoff and watch worker in `app.rs`, the log-before-run step in `serve`, a Settings field or two, and one dialog. Anything larger is proposed separately.
523	
524	## 13. Explicit design decisions
525	
526	| Decision | v1 choice |
527	|---|---|
528	| Topology | Independent hosts, no coordinator |
529	| Multi-host | Concurrent connections and unified browsing |
530	| Resources | Sessions, projects, working sets with pins, pinned files, runs; no card resource |
531	| Identity | `identity.json` UUID and certificate; key in the Keychain per installation; clients pin the public key |
532	| Discovery | Bonjour and manual endpoints |
533	| Host runtime | Frame-thread dispatch for core state; content work on connection and worker threads; blocking std server with bounded queues; no Tokio |
534	| Contract | The `switchboard-control` wire views, extended additively, behind an allowlist |
535	| Data fetch | HTTPS JSON, every reply stamped with epoch and revision |
536	| Live changes | One WSS per host; read-model diff after every pass, content versions assigned on read, watch worker; `changed`/`removed` events; refetch |
537	| Synchronization | Subscribe, then snapshot, then reconcile by revision; full refetch on a new epoch |
538	| Idempotency | The control port's operation id and `operations.log`, non-replayable commands logged before they run |
539	| Redaction | One policy over every text leaving the port, run on whole source text before any cut; fail closed |
540	| Caps | Collections answered whole with every string bounded; only the conversation pages; scalar content cut after masking or refused whole; the limit enforced on serialized bytes |
541	| Content versions | Transcript: size and mtime (append-only); file and run log: inode, ctime and size; screen: hash; no two bodies share a revision for one key |
542	| Masked caches | Versioned by source and by the project's redaction policy fingerprint; a resolution failure refuses, never serves a cached success |
543	| Watch set | Global cap of 128, least recently read evicted, never refused; a read always versions correctly |
544	| File reads | Descriptor-anchored `openat` walk, no symlink followed, nonblocking open, 768 KiB, on the connection thread |
545	| Authentication | Pairing window with QR, key verified before the code is sent, 40-bit single-use code with one global attempt counter, 256-bit bearer token without expiry, scope set in the host dialog; Keychain on both ends; key rotation clears every pairing |
546	| Client storage | Server list and presentation state on disk, token and pin in the Keychain, every host body in memory only |
547	| Milestone A | Five commits: cache move, authenticated read-only host, two-host client, synchronization, watched content |
548	| Session execution | Always on the owning host |
549	| Resume | User-initiated only, confirmed on the client |
550	| Presentation state | Client-owned |
551	| visionOS layout | Native movable windows |
552	| Remote internet access | Deferred; protocol-compatible |
553	| iPadOS | Shared Swift core and views |
